title: Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped | NOEMA
gist: Mike Mariani argues the widespread post-Covid feeling that time is accelerating is real and mechanistic: neuroscience has abandoned the “internal clock” model for one where the brain counts salient perceptual changes, so feed media both speeds up in-the-moment time and starves retrospective time of memories. Citing the TIMED consortium's three-year, tens-of-thousands-participant data, he claims heavy device use correlates with faster-feeling time, and that reclaiming boredom — not time management — is the fix.

insights.claim: A broad cross-generational belief has taken hold that time is moving faster than it did before the Covid pandemic, to the point that complaints about the speed of life are displacing small talk about the weather.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: A population-level shift in felt time is the demand backdrop for anything sold as attention reclamation, slow living, or time management.
insights.quote: There’s a growing conviction among people from all walks of life that time is moving faster than it did several decades ago — or even prior to the Covid pandemic.
insights.locator: You don’t have to look very far to find ample evidence

insights.claim: A 2023 Baylor University sociology study using Gallup data collected at the height of the pandemic found Americans experienced “time disorientation” in multiple directions at once — time speeding up, slowing down, and days blending into indistinguishability.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Peer-reviewed grounding that the pandemic distortion of felt time is measurable, not anecdote — the base case for studying attention-era time effects.
insights.locator: In 2023, researchers at Baylor University

insights.claim: A 2022 study in “Time & Society” of Uruguayan university students found 80% of those surveyed felt time had either sped up or slowed down during the pandemic, with findings replicated in Argentina and Iraq.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Cross-country replication suggests the effect is structural rather than culturally local — a global, not US-only, consumer phenomenon.
insights.locator: Another study of Uruguayan university students

insights.claim: Boredom produces an inverted time signature: empty, under-stimulating hours crawl in the moment but collapse retrospectively, because monotony encodes almost no memories — the pandemic lockdown was the worst-case combination of both.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Explains why ‘slow’ experiences can still feel like lost years; the retrospective channel, not the in-the-moment one, is what people grieve.
insights.quote: time would be slow in the moment, but looking back on the experience retrospectively, people would feel that time flew
insights.locator: The co-authors of the “Time & Society” paper

insights.claim: Marc Wittmann attributes pandemic time disorientation to the erasure of day-specific markers — the loss of ‘Monday is skating, Tuesday is friends’ structure — a condition he labels “Blursday.”
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
entities: Institute for Frontier Areas in Psychology and Mental Health
insights.so_what: Differentiated routine markers are the cheap intervention for felt-time collapse — relevant to any product selling structure, ritual, or scheduling.
insights.quote: Every day was the same
insights.locator: When I spoke to Marc Wittmann

insights.claim: The important question is no longer whether the pandemic warped time perception — that is settled by a raft of papers — but whether perception ever snapped back afterward, and the author argues it did not.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Frames the distortion as a permanent regime change rather than a transient shock, which is the bullish case for durable behavioral consequences.
insights.locator: But the most relevant question in 2026

insights.claim: Perception of time never reverted post-Covid because adoption of Slack, Teams and Zoom made work and home life porous, leaving minds permanently overstimulated by a low, 24-hour hum of productivity.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Names collaboration software as the mechanism of permanent time compression — a reputational and regulatory tail risk for always-on workplace tools.
insights.locator: This explains why many people feel

themes.theme: Age-Proportional vs Novelty Models of Duration

insights.claim: Paul Janet’s 1890s “logarithmic time perception” (or ‘time alive’) theory holds that a year is experienced in proportion to lifespan — 10% of life at age 10 versus 2% at age 50 — so the same interval feels progressively thinner with age.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: The oldest baseline explanation for accelerating time; if the felt-acceleration is cross-generational including Gen Z, age proportionality alone cannot be the driver.
insights.locator: In the 1890s, renowned French philosopher Paul Janet

insights.claim: William James argued that novelty, not age arithmetic, governs felt duration: young people slingshot into fresh experience daily, giving recollection an “intricate, multitudinous, and long-drawn-out” texture, while routine makes days smooth into contentless units.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: The actionable variable is novelty density, which is controllable at any age — unlike chronological age.
insights.quote: the days and the weeks smooth themselves out in recollection to contentless units, and the years grow hollow and collapse
insights.locator: William James picked up where Janet left off

insights.claim: Contemporary researchers now argue that how we gauge time is inextricably linked to how active and engaged our brains are and to the extent that memories form, validating James more than a century after he wrote before neuroscience or psychology existed as fields.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Memory formation, not clock time, is the variable to watch when assessing the felt cost of any attention product.
insights.quote: We only remember things which are novel or exciting or scary or have some visceral meaning to them
insights.locator: Though James was writing before the fields of neuroscience

themes.theme: Collapse Of The Internal Clock Model

insights.claim: Humans have no organ or system dedicated to sensing time; a 2016 paper frames psychological time as an abstraction or epiphenomenon of the mind’s functioning, created to explain the coherence of events.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: If there is no time organ, there is no biological floor — felt time is fully manipulable by environment design, for better or worse.
insights.quote: Psychological time is an abstraction, a construct or epiphenomenon of our mind’s functioning that we create in order to explain the coherence of events.
insights.locator: The Internal Clock Fallacy

insights.claim: Dean Buonomano argues the long-dominant “internal clock model” was an anthropocentric projection — an oscillator ticking and counting units, suspiciously similar to man-made clocks — and scientists never found the clock they spent years hunting for.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: A discredited dominant model means the field is mid-paradigm-shift; findings built on the old model deserve discount.
insights.quote: Back then, there was a very anthropocentric model that was suspiciously similar to actual man-made clocks
insights.locator: Nevertheless, researchers were convinced for years

insights.claim: A 2022 University of Sussex study by Warrick Roseboom and colleagues showed participants short videos and found brain activity tied to visual processing was strongly correlated with subjective duration — time is told by “the accumulation of salient changes in the perceptual processing hierarchy.”
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Gives a measurable input variable — rate of salient perceptual change — that any media product directly controls.
insights.quote: the brain just ‘counts’ how much ‘stuff’ has happened, which is very intuitive
insights.locator: In 2022, he and several colleagues at the University of Sussex

insights.claim: Because the brain uses the external environment as a proxy for elapsed time, an information-saturated media diet mechanically accelerates subjective time: more ‘stuff’ registered by the sensory cortex equals more time registered as passing.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Direct causal link from content volume to felt acceleration — the mechanism behind any future ‘time harm’ critique of feed products.
insights.locator: One of the paper’s key takeaways

insights.claim: James Hyman applies the change-accumulation theory to the current media ecosystem: constant forward motion through content jams more countable things into the brain’s proxy mechanism, tricking it into speeding up.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Reframes feed velocity as a physiological time-tax, a framing that could migrate into product-design regulation.
insights.quote: if our brains are only able to tell time by counting things, then we’re jamming lots more things in there
insights.locator: When I reached out to James Hyman

themes.theme: The Memory Deficit Of Feed Media

insights.claim: Duration is judged on two separate channels with different inputs: in-the-moment speed depends on how engaged or stimulated you are, while retrospective speed depends almost entirely on how many vivid memories were formed.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: The core analytic lens of the piece: any product can win the in-the-moment channel while destroying the retrospective one — that gap is the harm.
insights.locator: This points to a crucial aspect of time perception

insights.claim: Digital media delivers the worst of both channels: apps flood the sensory cortex with visual information yet fail to generate the indelible experiences memory requires, so the day ends as an undifferentiated blur despite heavy stimulation.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the naive prediction of Roseboom’s theory — the strongest intellectual move in the essay and the crux of the anti-feed case.
insights.quote: But I think we’ve got the worst of all worlds
insights.locator: Our memories are the key to the central irony

insights.claim: Wittmann argues that app-toggling and Instagram reels impoverish retrospective time because the experiences cannot be encoded and later recalled — they simply vanish.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Puts memory encodability, not screen time alone, as the metric that separates harmful from benign digital use.
insights.quote: You’re jumping around like mad in these apps, and you can’t put them into memory and later recall them, because the experiences just vanish.
insights.locator: Wittmann agrees that toggling between apps

insights.claim: An hour on TikTok may feel like 10 or 15 minutes because scrolling anesthetizes rather than activates the brain, and the author extrapolates that heavy daily social media use can make a full day feel like only 12 or 13 waking hours.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Quantifies the felt-time cost of feed consumption — a framing that could power a consumer backlash narrative against engagement-maximizing apps.
insights.locator: Browsing, scrolling and swiping

insights.claim: The second-order consequence of memory-free digital hours is a sense of deprivation — the feeling that years have been carved out of one’s life — leaving people confined to a permanent amnesiac present.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Frames the harm as cumulative and biographical rather than per-session, which is the shape of harms that eventually attract litigation and regulation.
insights.quote: many of us are now confined to a permanent amnesiac present, one throbbing with artificial life but unable to fathom where it came from or where it’s going
insights.locator: According to Wittmann and other researchers

insights.claim: Time Experience in Europe’s Digital Age (TIMED), a consortium of top time-perception researchers in Germany, Spain, Switzerland and the U.K., has spent three years collecting data from tens of thousands of participants worldwide on how technology use shapes time perception.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: A named, large-N research program now publishing — the likely evidentiary source for future policy arguments about screen time.
insights.locator: Investigating The Time Warp

insights.claim: TIMED’s first published finding is that people who spend more time on devices and social media platforms experience time passing more quickly, with memory identified as the key mediating factor — routine app-checking crowds out novel, embodied experiences that would be encoded in autobiographical memory.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: The empirical anchor linking device usage to felt time loss; watch for this to be cited in screen-time regulation and platform litigation.
insights.quote: Routine activities such as repeatedly checking apps or prolonged online engagement for professional purposes could reduce the frequency of novel, embodied, and enactive experiences
insights.locator: In papers published so far

insights.claim: TIMED found that heavy device use produces a distinctly negative relationship with time — a sense of losing it, a compulsion to fill all of it, a tendency to forget it — which in turn spawns feelings of guilt, shame and a lack of self-control.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Guilt and shame are the emotional substrate of consumer backlash; when users blame a product for lost time, churn and regulation follow.
insights.quote: feelings of guilt, shame, and a lack of self-control
insights.locator: Unsurprisingly, perhaps, researchers also found

insights.claim: Ruth Ogden reports that doom scrolling abolishes awareness of time entirely, which is precisely why users massively overextend how long they engage — participants described digital technology as ‘stealing their time.’
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Time-blindness is the mechanism converting session design into session length — the engagement metric and the harm are the same variable.
insights.quote: you completely forget about time — time doesn’t exist anymore. So then you massively overextend how long you engage in these activities for
insights.locator: Wittmann and his colleagues conducted qualitative interviews

insights.claim: Ogden refuses to blame technology alone: TIMED interviews found people are uncomfortable with inactivity and fill every gap in their schedule with screens, because the culture values constant busyness — the device is the instrument, not the cause.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: If cultural demand for busyness drives usage, device-limiting features and app timers will underperform expectations as remedies.
insights.quote: even when people have time, they don’t use it to do nothing
insights.locator: But Ogden doesn’t think that technology should be seen as the sole culprit

insights.claim: Gen Z in particular does not discuss the quickening pace of life with detached curiosity but laments it, and TIMED shows people who feel they are losing time are genuinely unhappy and distressed.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: The most digitally native cohort is the most distressed by the effect — a leading indicator for shifting attitudes toward attention products.
insights.locator: The Beauty Of Boredom

insights.claim: Ogden argues society has placed too much responsibility on individuals to limit technology use and that the burden should shift to creators, explicitly targeting the industry’s core success metric — how long users stay on and how many can be kept on as long as possible.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: A direct normative attack on time-on-app as a success metric; if this framing gains traction it pressures the engagement-based ad model itself.
insights.quote: The key metric for the success of digital technology is how long users are on it for, and how many people they can get on it for as long as possible. How do we flip that?
insights.locator: For their part, Ogden and other TIMED researchers

insights.claim: James Hyman says calm, unproductive moments show a unique pattern of activity in the brain region responsible for making memories, meaning idle time is functionally required for memory consolidation rather than merely pleasant.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Gives a neuroscientific justification for deliberate idleness — the mechanism behind why ‘doing nothing’ products and practices may have real efficacy.
insights.quote: It’s in those calm moments where we see a unique pattern of activity in the part of our brain responsible for helping to make our memories
insights.locator: If people were more comfortable with intervals that lacked so-called productivity

insights.claim: The author argues the time-acceleration crisis is reversible in principle: since felt speed tracks the volume of information the brain engages with, deliberately cutting daily stimuli will gradually slow the brain and taper the sense of time.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: The falsifiable, testable prescription of the piece — stimulus reduction as an intervention, and the thesis underlying digital-detox demand.
insights.locator: If we accept this premise

insights.claim: Jenny Odell frames the contest over attention as “a battle playing out for our time, a colonization of the self by capitalist ideas of productivity and efficiency,” with device makers supplying the badges and motifs that signify enterprising competence.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: The ideological frame that turns time-warping from a personal failing into a systemic critique of productivity-tool marketing.
insights.quote: for our time, a colonization of the self by capitalist ideas of productivity and efficiency
insights.locator: It’s true that technology has capitalized on this culture

insights.claim: Post-pandemic, pre-Covid competitive trends resurfaced ‘shot out of a cannon’ — racing to make money, afford a home, secure a job, and make up for lost live events — imbuing the culture with a mercenary quality that made everything move faster.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Attributes felt acceleration partly to economic scarcity and catch-up consumption, not only to screens — a demand driver for experience spending.
insights.locator: Further, trends that predated Covid resurfaced

insights.claim: William James’s experiment of closing your eyes and waiting to be told a minute has elapsed shows that unstimulated time feels overwhelmingly long, because “the feeling of bare time” is the least stimulating experience available — stimulation compresses and disguises duration.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: A free, self-administered test of the whole thesis; the inverse relationship between stimulation and felt duration is the model to reason from.
insights.quote: The feeling of bare time
insights.locator: In his “Principles of Psychology,” William James invites us

insights.claim: The everyday dead-time intervals that once forced unstimulated waiting — grocery lines, gazing out an airplane window, watching an oven timer count down — are now endangered, and the author claims they were far more valuable than anyone realized.
insights.speaker: MIKE MARIANI
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific micro-moments smartphones eliminated; their disappearance is the concrete unit of the loss being described.
insights.quote: These are now the endangered species of our day-to-day lives. And they are far more valuable than we ever could have known.
insights.locator: We used to tolerate those interminable minutes
